about: The two boys' plan works. The old man and the old woman come to Vucub Caquix's house with the boys playing behind them, and the macaw, crying out with the pain of his teeth, asks where they come from; they say they are old people seeking their living, and that the boys are their grandsons. Hearing that they draw the worms out of teeth and heal eyes, he begs them to cure him. They tell him the worm must come out and new 'smooth bone' go in, and he agrees; but the new teeth are only grains of white maize. His face falls, he no longer looks like a lord; his jewelled teeth come out, his eyes are worked on, his silver is taken, and he dies. Hunahpu takes back his arm, Chimalmat dies too, and the old pair, beings of spirit power, set the boys' arm back in place. Then the story turns to Zipacna, the elder son, who calls himself the maker of mountains. While he is bathing he meets four hundred boys who cannot lift the great tree they have cut for the ridge-beam of their house; he carries it to their door on his shoulder. They ask him to stay with them, and then, afraid of his strength, they plot to kill him: they dig a deep pit, send him down to dig it deeper, and mean to drop the great tree on him. Zipacna knows what they intend and digs himself a second hole at the side to be safe in, and calls up from the pit that he is still digging.

sentences.t: Cate cut ta xebec ꜩamal cubi ri Vucub Caquix chuvach vcalibal;
sentences.l: Then then when they-went end(?) lying(?) the Seven Macaw before his-seat(?);
sentences.i: Then they set off for the far end, where Vucub Caquix lay before his seat;
sentences.n: The old couple and the boys go to the macaw's house, as they agreed at the end of the last part. xebec 'they went': x- (completed action) + e 'they' + be 'go' + -c, as xbec in the last part. ꜩamal 'the end, the far end' is taken from ꜩam 'tip' (the tip of the shoulder in the last part) with -al; cubi 'lying, seated' is not otherwise known. Both follow Brasseur's French ('to the far end, where Vucub Caquix lay in front of his throne') and are inferred. vcalibal 'his seat': v- 'his' + calibal, the seat of the macaw's boast in the earlier part ('my seat is silver'), a noun of place in -ibal; Brasseur reads the letter as ꜫ (u galibal), but Ximénez writes plain c, and the toggle respells the letters as written, as there. Whether a throne is meant is inferred from Brasseur. In Vucub, here and throughout the part, the second letter often looks like v (Vvcub); it is printed Vucub, as in the last part.

sentences.t: ta xe icouic ri atit, mama, que eꜩeyah cu ri e caib ꜭaholab chiquih;
sentences.l: when they-passed the old-woman, old-man, they playing(?) then the they two boys behind-them;
sentences.i: the old woman and the old man passed by, and the two boys were playing behind them;
sentences.n: xe icouic 'they passed': x- + e 'they' (the absolutive, the person of an intransitive verb) + icou 'pass' + -ic, the ending of an intransitive verb at the end of its clause. The manuscript has plain c in all three forms of this verb in the part, where Brasseur reads q (that is ꜭ); the verb is the certain ik'ow 'pass', so the toggle shows ik'owik. This is the establishment log's first doubtful reading. atit, mama 'old woman, old man', the pair of the last part; the ti of atit is the ß-ligature, read ti here and throughout, as there. que eꜩeyah 'they were playing': que is c- (ongoing) + e 'they'; eꜩeyah is taken as 'play' with Brasseur ('playing behind them'), and the form is not otherwise known; the image has the plain tz ligature, and the toggle respells it etzeyaj. chiquih 'behind them': chi + qu- + ih 'back'. In the last part the same letters were chiquih 'behind us' (ca- 'our' before a vowel); here the boys are behind the old couple, so the qu is k-, the form of qui- 'their' before a vowel, and the toggle shows chikij.

sentences.t: ta xe icou chuxe rochoch ahau, cu racuh cu vchi ri Vucub Caquix rumal re.
sentences.l: when they-passed at-foot-of his-house lord, he-scraped(?) then his-mouth the Seven Macaw because-of his-teeth.
sentences.i: and as they passed at the foot of the lord's house, Vucub Caquix was crying out because of his teeth.
sentences.n: xe icou, the same verb without -ic, because more follows in the clause; the manuscript runs taxei-|cou across a line. chuxe rochoch ahau 'at the foot of the lord's house': chuxe 'at the foot of' (chi + v- + xe 'root, foot'), rochoch 'his house' (r- + ochoch). ahau 'lord, ruler' (modern ajaw), the title the macaw is given throughout this part. cu racuh cu vchi 'he was crying out', word for word 'he scraped his mouth', as chu racuh vchi in the last part (Brasseur's note gives the same words as 'he cried out'); the first cu is c- (ongoing) + v- 'he', the second is taken as the particle 'then', and the sense is inferred. rumal re 'because of his teeth': re is r- 'his' + e 'tooth', not the re 'of' of the earlier parts (Brasseur 'because of his teeth').

sentences.t: Ta xil cut Vucub Caquix ri mama, atit, cachbilan quib.
sentences.l: Then saw then Seven Macaw the old-man, old-woman, accompanying themselves.
sentences.i: Then Vucub Caquix saw the old man and the old woman, and those who came with them.
sentences.n: xil 'he saw': x- + il 'see', with no prefix for 'he' written (one would expect xril; compare xmeho in the last part). cachbilan quib 'accompanying one another, who came along together': c- (ongoing) + achbilan 'accompany', the verb of the last part, + quib 'themselves'. In the last part cachbilan was 'we accompany' (c- for ca- 'we' before a vowel), and the toggle showed qachb'ilan; here the narrator speaks, and the c is taken as the ongoing k-, so the toggle shows kachb'ilan. Brasseur reads 'and those who accompanied them'. The reading is inferred.

sentences.t: “Apa quix pe vi, ca mam?” xꜭha cu ri ahau.
sentences.l: “Where you(pl.)-come from there, our grandfathers?” said then the lord.
sentences.i: “Where do you come from, grandfathers?” said the lord.
sentences.n: Apa 'where' asks the place, and vi points back to it: 'where ... from'. quix pe 'you (pl.) come': c- + ix 'you (pl.)' + pe 'come'. ca mam 'our grandfathers': ca- 'our'. mam is the old man of the family and also the grandson; the macaw speaks to the old pair as elders, and they will answer with the same word for the boys. xꜭha 'he said' (x- + ꜭha 'say'): the manuscript's gh is read ꜭh here and in every xꜭha, xeꜭha, caꜭha, ꜭhauic and xuꜭhaxic of this part.

sentences.t: “Xa oh ꜩucubei quib, lal ahau,” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “Only we seeking-sustenance(?) ourselves, you lord,” they-said then.
sentences.i: “We are only seeking our living, my lord,” they said.
sentences.n: oh 'we'. ꜩucubei is taken as 'seeking (something) to live on', with Brasseur, whose note derives it from ꜩucuh 'sustain, feed'; the ending -ei is not clear. The root is tzuq 'feed', with q (Brasseur's k is q), as in ꜩucul 'provider' (tzuqul) of the first part, and the toggle shows tzuqub'ei. quib here is 'ourselves': ca- 'our' becomes q- before a vowel, so q- + ib 'self' is written quib, with the same letters as quib 'themselves' (two lines up). lal 'you', the respectful word for one person, used to a lord; with ahau it makes 'my lord'.

sentences.t: “Naquipa iꜩucubal? Ma ivalcual ri ivachbilan?”
sentences.l: “What your-sustenance? Not(?) your-children the you-accompany?”
sentences.i: “What do you live on? Are these your children, whom you have with you?”
sentences.n: The lord asks two questions. iꜩucubal 'your means of living': i- 'your (pl.)' + ꜩucub (as above, toggle tzuqub') + -al. Ma opens a question here, as in the earlier parts. ivalcual 'your children': iv- 'your (pl.)', the form before a vowel, + alcual 'children', built on al 'a woman's child' (Brasseur 'are these your children'). The word is certain, the modern alk'wal, so the toggle restores the ejective that Ximénez leaves unmarked and shows iwalk'wal. The manuscript runs maiv alcual together; it is divided Ma + ivalcual, as the establishment log says, with iv- as in ivachbilan 'you accompany' (iv- + achbilan, the verb above).

sentences.t: “Mahabi, lal ahau; e ca mam ri;
sentences.l: “None, you lord; they our grandsons these;
sentences.i: “No, my lord; they are our grandsons;
sentences.n: Mahabi 'there is none, no'. e ca mam ri 'they are our grandsons': e 'they' before a noun, with no verb, as e cabauil 'they (were) gods' in the last part; ri 'these' closes it. mam here is the grandson, the young end of the line, as in the boys' plan in the last part: the old couple say what the boys told them to say.

sentences.t: xere nare ca ca tocobah qui vach, ri yaaxel hupir chacap ca caya chiquech, lal ahau,” xeꜭha cut ri atit, mama.
sentences.l: only-so nare(?) we-pity their face, the yaaxel(?) one-part(?) half(?) we-give to-them, you lord,” they-said then the old-woman, old-man.
sentences.i: we only take pity on them, and a share, a half of what we have, we give to them, my lord,” said the old woman and the old man.
sentences.n: ca ca tocobah qui vach 'we pity them', word for word 'we pity their faces' (Brasseur's note): the first ca is the ongoing c- written apart, the second is ca- 'we'; the second ca is written above the line in the manuscript and is printed in its place. tocobah 'pity, have mercy on'; Ximénez writes plain c, Brasseur tokobah (his k is q) here and togobah (g, that is ꜫ) two lines below. The word is the certain toq'ob' 'pity', and the toggle shows toq'ob'aj, with the ejective restored. nare is not explained (Brasseur 'but you see'). ri yaaxel hupir chacap ca caya chiquech: ca caya 'we give' (ca + ca- 'we' + ya 'give'), chiquech 'to them'. yaaxel is clear in the image but its meaning is unknown, as the establishment log says; hupir (hun 'one' + pir) and chacap are taken as 'a part, a half' from Brasseur's French ('we share and give them half'). The whole clause is inferred: the old pair share their food with the boys.

sentences.t: Cuꜩin cu ri ahau rumal vcoxom ve; xa cu nimac vachih chic ca ꜭhauic:
sentences.l: Was-finished then the lord because-of its-aching(?) teeth; only then great vachih(?) now he-speaking:
sentences.i: The lord was at the end of his strength from the pain of his teeth; it was only with great effort that he spoke:
sentences.n: Cuꜩin 'he is at an end': c- (ongoing) + vꜩin 'be finished', from vꜩ 'good, complete' (Brasseur 'the king was at the end'); inferred. vcoxom ve 'the aching of his teeth': coxom is the coxou 'ache' of the last part with -om; ve 'teeth', as in the macaw's boast (Brasseur u e 'his teeth'). nimac vachih is taken as 'with great effort' from Brasseur, who prints one word; vachih is not otherwise known. ca ꜭhauic 'he was speaking': ca + ꜭhau 'speak' + -ic. Ximénez struck through a few letters before ca; they are not printed.

sentences.t: “In ta ba canih chivech; chi tocobah ta nu vach.
sentences.l: “I then then canih(?) to-you(pl.); (please) pity then my face.
sentences.i: “I beg you, then: have pity on me.
sentences.n: canih chivech is taken as a word of entreaty, 'I beg you' (Brasseur's French has 'I implore you'; in a note on the same word later in this part he gives 'love'); its sense is inferred. chivech 'to you (pl.)': chi + iv- 'your (pl.)' + ech. chi tocobah ta nu vach 'have pity on my face', that is, on me: chi is ch-, the prefix of a command, + i- 'you (pl.)', as Brasseur writes it (ch'y tokobah) and as in chivelezah below; ta softens it. ba, a particle of urging, not otherwise explained.

sentences.t: Naquipa qui chi bano, naquion qui chi cunah?” xꜭha cut ahau.
sentences.l: What things you-do, which things you-cure?” said then lord.
sentences.i: What is it you do? What is it you cure?” said the lord.
sentences.n: A couplet of questions. naquipa, naquion 'what, which'. chi bano, chi cunah: chi is read as ch- + i- 'you (pl.)', as Brasseur writes it (ch'y bano); qui before it is taken as marking the questioned things as many ('what things'), after his French ('what things do you cure'); both are inferred. After naquion Ximénez wrote ch at the end of the line and struck it; it is not printed. cunah 'cure, heal' (modern kunaj), the root of ahꜭun 'healer' below.

sentences.t: “Xa vchicopil eiah chi quelezah, xa cu vbac vvach chi ca cunah, xa bac chi ca vico, lal ahau,” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “Only its-animals teeth we-take-out, only then its-bone its-face we-cure, only bone we-set(?), you lord,” they-said then.
sentences.i: “We only draw the worms out of teeth, we only cure the eyes, we only set bones, my lord,” they said.
sentences.n: Three trades in three parallel lines, each led by xa 'only': the healers' modest answer. vchicopil eiah 'the animals of the teeth', the worms believed to cause toothache, as in the boys' plan in the last part. quelezah 'we take out': q- (ca- 'we' before a vowel) + elezah 'take out' (el 'go out' + -ez-, which makes a verb 'cause to ...', + -ah). vbac vvach 'the bone of the face' is the eye, the eyeball (Brasseur 'the globe of the eye'). vico 'set (bones)' is not otherwise known and is inferred from Brasseur ('we put the bones back'). In each line chi stands before the verb.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala. Chi cunah ta ba ve quiꜩih ca coxouic hutaꜫih; maui choꜫitahic, mahabi nu varam rumal, ruꜭ vbac nu vach.
sentences.l: “Good bala. (Please) cure then then my-teeth, truly they-ache every-day; not choꜫitahic(?), there-is-none my-sleep because-of-it, with its-bone my face.
sentences.i: “Very well. Cure my teeth, then, for truly they ache every day; I have no rest, I have no sleep because of them, nor because of my eyes.
sentences.n: Vꜩ bala 'very well', as at the end of the last part. Chi cunah 'cure!': ch- (command) + i- 'you (pl.)' + cunah (Brasseur ch'y cunah). ve 'my teeth': v- 'my' + e 'tooth'. ca coxouic 'they ache' (ca + coxou + -ic), the coxou of the last part. hutaꜫih 'every day' (hun 'one' + tac 'each' + ꜫih 'day'); the q-shaped letter is read ꜫ (Brasseur g), here and in choꜫitahic. maui choꜫitahic, mahabi nu varam 'no rest, no sleep for me', a couplet: choꜫitahic is not otherwise known and 'rest' follows Brasseur (ch'ogitahic); nu varam 'my sleep': nu 'my' + varam 'sleep', from var 'sleep' (the root of vvarabal 'its place to sleep') + -am. ruꜭ vbac nu vach 'with the bone of my face', the eyes: the pain of the eyes is added to the teeth.

sentences.t: Xa xi quivbah e caib ꜭaxtoꜭ ta xticaric; maui quin echahic rumal.
sentences.l: Only me they-blowgunned they two demons when it-began; not I eat because-of-it.
sentences.i: It was two demons who shot me with the blowgun to begin with; I cannot eat because of it.
sentences.n: xi quivbah 'they shot me with the blowgun', as xi quivubah in the last part, here written without the u: x- + i(n) 'me' (the absolutive object, its n not written) + qui- 'they' (the ergative subject) + vbah, the verb made from vb 'blowgun'. ꜭaxtoꜭ 'demons', the macaw's word for the boys, both letters g-shaped and read ꜭ. ta xticaric 'when it began', taken as 'to begin with' (Brasseur). maui quin echahic 'I do not eat': quin is c- + in 'I'; echahic is from echa 'food' (recha 'his food' in the last part) with -h- + -ic, 'eating'; inferred.

sentences.t: Quehe ta cut chi tocobah vi nu vach; xa ca chuiub vehe chic ri ve.”
sentences.l: Thus then then pity there my face; only they-are loose(?) my-gums(?) now the my-teeth.”
sentences.i: So have pity on me; my gums and my teeth are loose now.”
sentences.n: Quehe ta cut 'so then'. chi tocobah vi nu vach 'have pity on me', as above (ch- + i- 'you (pl.)'; Brasseur ch'y togobah). xa ca chuiub vehe chic ri ve is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has chuiub vehe (Brasseur ch'u yub v'ehe). chuiub is taken as the chuiu 'loose' of the macaw's complaint in the last part, and vehe as v- 'my' + ehe, the ahe 'gums' of that line; the meaning ('they are all loose') is inferred, as the establishment log says. ri ve 'my teeth'.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala, lal ahau. Chicop ba ca cuxuuic; xa choc vꜫexel, chel ri e la.”
sentences.l: “Good bala, you lord. Animal then it-aches(?); only let-enter its-replacement, let-go-out the teeth your(sir).”
sentences.i: “Very well, my lord. It is a worm that makes them ache; only let their replacement go in, and let Your Lordship's teeth come out.”
sentences.n: Chicop 'animal', here the worm in the tooth. ca cuxuuic: the manuscript has cacuxuuic, where earlier on the page it has ca coxouic, and Brasseur prints ca coxuvic; it is printed as written and taken as the same verb 'ache' (doubtful reading). xa choc vꜫexel, chel ri e la 'only let its replacement go in, let the teeth come out', a couplet of opposites: choc is ch- (wish) + oc 'enter' (modern ok, with k, as xoc 'entered' → xok in the earlier parts), chel is ch- + el 'go out'. vꜫexel 'its replacement, what is put in exchange': the manuscript writes a q-shaped letter + u (vquexel), read ꜫ with Brasseur (u gexel), here and twice more; the modern word for 'replacement' is k'exel, but the toggle follows the manuscript's letter, as with vꜭhapa in the last part, and shows uq'exel. e 'teeth', with no possessor; la is the respectful 'you, Your Lordship' (as chi la in the last part).

sentences.t: “Maba vꜩ lo chel ri ve? Rumal xere in ahau vi, nu caubal ri ve, ruꜭ vbac nu vach.”
sentences.l: “Not-then good perhaps let-go-out the my-teeth? Because only-thus I lord there, my-beauty(?) the my-teeth, with its-bone my face.”
sentences.i: “Can it be good to take out my teeth? For only by them am I lord: my teeth are my beauty, with my eyes.”
sentences.n: Maba ... lo asks with doubt: ma (question) + ba, with lo 'perhaps'. chel ri ve 'that my teeth go out'. xere in ahau vi 'only thus am I lord': in ahau 'I (am) lord', with no verb. nu caubal 'my beauty, my adornment' is inferred from Brasseur ('all my beauty'), and caubal is not otherwise known. The macaw's greatness lies in his teeth and his eyes: his boast in the earlier parts was that his teeth shone like jewels and his eyes like silver.

sentences.t: “Xchi ca coh chic na cut vꜫexel, hocom bac; xchoc chic.”
sentences.l: “Shall we-put again now then its-replacement, smooth(?) bone; it-shall-enter again.”
sentences.i: “We will put in a replacement, smooth bone; it will go in again.”
sentences.n: Xchi ca coh 'we shall put': xchi- 'shall', the future prefix, written apart, + ca- 'we' + coh 'put, place' (as chi ca coh in the boys' plan). hocom bac 'smooth bone' (Brasseur 'pure and clean bones'); hocom is not otherwise known and is inferred, and Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has g. xchoc 'it shall go in': xch- (xchi before a vowel) + oc 'enter'.

sentences.t: Are cut hocom bac ri xa zaqui ixim.
sentences.l: This then smooth(?) bone the only white maize.
sentences.i: But the smooth bone was nothing but white maize.
sentences.n: The narrator lets the reader in on the trick. Are 'this (was)', with no verb. zaqui ixim 'white maize': zaqui 'white', the word of Zaqui Nimac's name. Ximénez wrote an x before ri and struck it; it is not printed.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala; chivelezah, chi too vloc,” xꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “Good bala; take-them-out(pl.), help(?) hither,” said then.
sentences.i: “Very well: take them out, and come to my help,” he said.
sentences.n: chivelezah 'take (them) out!': ch- (command) + iv- 'you (pl.)' + elezah. chi too vloc is taken as 'help (me)', with Brasseur ('come to my aid'); too is printed as written (MS chi|too vloc, across a line), and its form is a doubtful reading. The double vowel may stand for a glottal stop, as elsewhere in Ximénez's spelling.

sentences.t: Ta xel cu ri re Vucub Caquix;
sentences.l: Then went-out then the his-teeth Seven Macaw;
sentences.i: Then the teeth of Vucub Caquix came out;
sentences.n: xel 'they went out': x- + el 'go out', with no -ic, because more follows in the clause (as xe icou above). re 'his teeth', r- + e, as in the first lines of this part.

sentences.t: xa zaqui ixim vꜫexel re xoquic, xa chi cu zac huluhuh chi vla ixim pu chi.
sentences.l: only white maize its-replacement his-teeth entered; only (chi) then white shining(?) (chi) hither maize also mouth.
sentences.i: only white maize went in to replace his teeth, and at once the maize shone white in his mouth.
sentences.n: xoquic 'it went in': x- + oc 'enter' + -ic. vꜫexel re 'the replacement of his teeth'. zac huluhuh is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has zac at the end of a line and huluhuh on the next, with no hyphen, and Brasseur prints one word, zakhuluhuh; it is divided here. The same word is the zachuluhuh of the macaw's boast in the fourth part (nu ꜩam zachuluhuh 'my nose gleams white', of his beak), written there as one word. zac is 'white'; huluhuh is taken as 'gleaming', after Brasseur ('these grains of maize shone in his mouth'), and is inferred. The z of zac has a long tail that looks like a cedilla. vla 'hither', as in the third part; chi 'mouth', as in vchi 'his mouth'.

sentences.t: Huzucu xcah vvach, maui ahau chic xvachinic.
sentences.l: Suddenly fell his-face, not lord now he-appeared.
sentences.i: At once his face fell, and he no longer looked like a lord.
sentences.n: Huzucu 'suddenly, at once': the manuscript has Huzu-|cu across a line, where the last part printed huzuc; it is printed as written. xcah 'it went down': x- + cah 'descend' (modern qaj; Brasseur x-kah, his k is q), Brasseur 'his splendour fell at once'. The third part gave this verb kaj in xcahixic 'were brought down'; the verb is qaj, and it is qaj throughout this part. vvach 'his face'. xvachinic 'he showed himself, he appeared': x- + vachin, from vach 'face', + -ic.

sentences.t: Xquiz elic ri re, caual, raxcanacoh pu chi.
sentences.l: Finished coming-out the his-teeth, precious-stones(?), shining-green(?) also mouth.
sentences.i: His teeth came out to the last, the precious stones that shone green in his mouth.
sentences.n: xquiz elic 'they finished coming out': x- + quiz 'end, be finished' (the quizoc of the boys' plan; the toggle shows k'is, the certain verb) + el 'go out' + -ic. caual is taken as the precious stone of the macaw's boast (raxa cuval, vcual), here written with a. Brasseur prints qual here and in the healer's line below, as he printed vcual in the last part. There the toggle showed ukuwal, because a letter was missing from cuval; here a letter is different, so the toggle respells the letters as written (kawal). The sense is inferred (Brasseur 'his teeth of precious stones'). raxcanacoh is the raxcavacoh 'shining blue-green' of the macaw's boast, here with n (Brasseur, OCR, raxcauacoh); not otherwise known. pu chi 'and in his mouth'.

sentences.t: Ta xcunax chi cut vbac vvach Vucub Caquix; ta xcholic vbac vvach, xquiz elic ri puvac.
sentences.l: Then was-cured in-turn then its-bone his-face Seven Macaw; when was-cholic(?) its-bone his-face, finished coming-out the silver.
sentences.i: Then the eyes of Vucub Caquix were treated; and when his eyes were stripped, all his silver was gone.
sentences.n: xcunax 'it was cured': x- + cunah 'cure' + -x, the passive, as the -ax- of vvbaxic 'his being shot with the blowgun'. vbac vvach 'the bone of his face', his eyes. chi cut is chic 'in turn' with its c shared with cut, as in the earlier parts. xcholic is not otherwise known; Brasseur's French has the eyes 'flayed', and 'stripped' is a guess. ri puvac 'the silver', the metal of his eyes in his boast: with his teeth and his eyes he loses all he gloried in.

sentences.t: Mana ca xtah xunao; xaui xere ca mucunic, ta xquiz cu elic ri vnimarizabal rib, xaui qui naoh ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: Not now heard(?) he-felt; only only-so he-was looking(?), when finished then coming-out the his-making-great himself, only their thought the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: He did not feel it any more; he only looked on, while all that made him great was taken from him, all by the counsel of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Mana 'not'. xtah xunao: xunao 'he felt': x- + v- 'he' + na 'feel, perceive' + -o, the ending of a transitive verb (the root of naoh 'thought'); the toggle shows xunao, as xca nao 'we felt' in the fourth part. xtah is not clear; it may be x- + ta 'hear', 'he did not hear, did not feel', but this is a guess. Brasseur has 'he was no longer able to feel it'. xaui xere ca mucunic 'he only looked on': mucunic 'looking on', as in the fourth part, inferred. vnimarizabal rib 'his making himself great', the nimarizabal of the last part with v- 'his' and rib 'himself'. xaui qui naoh 'only (by) their counsel': the old couple's work was the boys' plan.

sentences.t: Ta xcam cut ri Vucub Caquix, ta xucam cut vꜫab ri Hunahpu.
sentences.l: Then died then the Seven Macaw, when took then his-arm the Hunahpu.
sentences.i: Then Vucub Caquix died, and Hunahpu took back his arm.
sentences.n: Two verbs written alike: xcam 'he died' (x- + cam 'die', modern kam), and xucam 'he took' (x- + v- 'he' + cam 'take', modern k'am), the verb of xquicam in the last part. The prefix v- marks the second as transitive; Brasseur prints q (that is ꜭ) in the second only, and the toggle shows kam and k'am. vꜫab 'his arm', with the tresillo: the arm the macaw tore off and hung over the fire. Here the boy is Hunahpu again, not Hunhunahpu.

sentences.t: Xcam nai puch Chimalmat, rixoquil Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: Died likewise also Chimalmat, his-wife Seven Macaw.
sentences.i: Chimalmat too died, the wife of Vucub Caquix.
sentences.n: nai puch 'likewise, also'. Chimalmat, the macaw's wife, named in the last part as the mother of Zipacna and Cabracan.

sentences.t: Quehe cut vzachic vꜫinomal Vucub Caquix; ri xa ahꜭun xcamouic ri caual, yamanic, xupunabeh varal chuvach vleu.
sentences.l: Thus then its-loss his-wealth Seven Macaw; the only healer was-the-one-who-took the precious-stones(?), jewels, he-punabeh(?) here on-face-of earth.
sentences.i: Such was the loss of the wealth of Vucub Caquix: it was only a healer who took the precious stones, the jewels he had been proud of here on the face of the earth.
sentences.n: vzachic 'its loss' (zach 'be lost' + -ic) and vꜫinomal 'his wealth', both from the last part; in vꜫinomal the q-shaped letter is read ꜫ (Brasseur g). ahꜭun 'healer, doctor': ah 'he of, one who' + ꜭun, the cun of cunah 'cure' above. The manuscript has ahgun, and the g-shaped letter is read ꜭ by the letter rule, as the establishment log says; the word is the healer word, modern ajkun with plain k, and Brasseur prints c (aheun in the OCR, that is ahcun), but the toggle follows the manuscript's letter, as with vꜫexel above and vꜭhapa in the last part, and shows ajk'un. xcamouic 'it was he who took': x- + cam 'take' + -ou- + -ic; the ending -ou- marks the verb when the doer is set in front of it for emphasis ('it was the healer who took'). Brasseur reads q (that is ꜭ), and with the sense clear the toggle shows k'am. In the last part xcamou chi la, the same verb without -ic, was left kamow, its sense unclear there. caual, yamanic 'precious stones, jewels', the pair of the boys' plan (vcual, vyamanic), inferred as there. xupunabeh is not otherwise known; 'he was proud of' follows Brasseur ('which he gloried in') and is inferred.

sentences.t: Naual atit, naual mama xbanouic.
sentences.l: Spirit-power old-woman, spirit-power old-man was-the-ones-who-did(-it).
sentences.i: It was an old woman of spirit power, an old man of spirit power who did it.
sentences.n: naual 'spirit power' (modern nawal), the word of the house table: the old pair were not ordinary people. The couplet sets each one under the same word. xbanouic 'it was they who did it': x- + ban 'do' + -ou- + -ic, the same ending as xcamouic, because the doers come first. Before this line about ten lines of the manuscript are struck through by Ximénez, a passage apparently copied out of place; they are not printed.

sentences.t: Ta xquicam cut qui ꜫab, xtiquitax vcoc, vꜩ chic xuxic.
sentences.l: Then they-took then their arm, was-planted(?) its-entering(?), good again it-became.
sentences.i: Then they took up the boys' arm; it was set back in place, and it was whole again.
sentences.n: xquicam 'they took': x- + qui- 'they' + cam 'take' (Brasseur qam, read k'am as in the last part). qui ꜫab 'their arm': the boys' arm, Hunahpu's, the boys counted as one, as in the last part; the manuscript writes quiꜫab with the tresillo. xtiquitax vcoc is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has xßquitax v-|coc, the ß-ligature read ti, and Brasseur prints x-tiqui ta x-uq-oc; xtiquitax is taken as x- + tiqui 'plant, set' (as in tiquiba 'plant, begin') + -tax, a passive, and vcoc as 'its going in'; 'it was set, it went in' is inferred. vꜩ chic xuxic 'it became good again' (xuxic 'it came to be').

sentences.t: Xa rumal vcamic Vucub Caquix xcah quehe xquibano; iꜩel xquilo nimarizabal ib.
sentences.l: Only because-of his-death Seven Macaw they-wanted thus they-did; evil they-saw making-great self.
sentences.i: Only for the death of Vucub Caquix did they want to do this: they saw it as evil, his making himself great.
sentences.n: vcamic 'his death' (cam 'die' + -ic). xcah 'they wanted': x- + c- (qui- 'their' before a vowel) + ah 'want', the ah of xrah 'he wanted' (Brasseur 'they wished to act so'). These are the same letters as xcah 'it went down' above, read differently, and the toggle shows xkaj here and xqaj there. iꜩel xquilo 'they saw (it) as evil', as at the beginning of the last part. nimarizabal ib 'making oneself great': ib 'self', here with no possessor.

sentences.t: Cate cut xebec chic e caib ꜭaholab; xa vꜩih ri Vꜭux Cah ta xquibano.
sentences.l: Then then went again they two boys; only its-word the Heart of-Sky when they-did.
sentences.i: Then the two boys went on their way again; what they did was only the word of the Heart of Sky.
sentences.n: xebec chic 'they went on again'. vꜩih 'its word' (ꜩih 'word'). Vꜭux Cah 'Heart of Sky', the creator whose word the boys obey (the last part: the macaw wanted to be great 'before the Heart of Sky'). ta xquibano 'when they did (it)'.

sentences.t: Vae chi cute vbanoh chic Zipacna, vnabe ꜭahol Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: This (chi) then his-doing in-turn Zipacna, his-first son Seven Macaw.
sentences.i: Here, then, are the deeds of Zipacna, the first son of Vucub Caquix.
sentences.n: A large capital V begins the episode of Zipacna, and so a new paragraph. Vae 'this, here (is)', as at the start of the last part. vbanoh 'his doing, his deeds': v- + ban 'do' + -oh. The chi after Vae is not clear (Brasseur prints it too); chic 'in turn' follows. vnabe ꜭahol 'his first son': nabe 'first'.

sentences.t: “In banol huyub,” caꜭha ri Zipacna.
sentences.l: “I maker mountain,” he-says the Zipacna.
sentences.i: “I am the maker of the mountains,” Zipacna would say.
sentences.n: banol 'maker' (ban + -ol, the agent ending), as in his boast in the last part ('I am the maker of the earth'). caꜭha 'he says': ca (ongoing) + ꜭha 'say', a habit rather than one saying.

sentences.t: Are cu ri Zipacna catinic chu chi ha, ta xe icouic omuch ꜭaholab, e hur vi che racan qui cabal;
sentences.l: This then the Zipacna he-was-bathing at mouth water, when they-passed four-hundred boys, they dragging(?) there tree its-leg their house;
sentences.i: Zipacna was bathing at the water's edge when four hundred boys passed by, dragging a tree to be a post of their house;
sentences.n: catinic 'he was bathing': c- (ongoing) + atin 'bathe' + -ic; no prefix for 'he' is written, because 'he' of an intransitive verb has no mark (the e 'they' of xe icouic has one); the ß-ligature is read ti. chu chi ha 'at the edge of the water': chi 'mouth', so 'at the water's mouth'. omuch 'four hundred', twenty twenties, a round count of the vigesimal number system. e hur vi: the manuscript has ehurui, divided as Brasseur divides it (a doubtful reading); hur is taken as 'drag' with his French ('dragging a tree'). che racan qui cabal 'a tree (as) the leg of their house', that is, a post: racan 'its leg' (r- + acan). cabal 'house' follows Brasseur; the toggle respells the letters.

sentences.t: omuch chubinic, ta xquicat cut hun nima che, vvapalil qui cabal.
sentences.l: four-hundred walking(?), when they-cut then one great tree, its-ridge-beam their house.
sentences.i: four hundred of them walking along; they had cut a great tree for the ridge-beam of their house.
sentences.n: omuch chubinic 'four hundred walking (together)': bin 'walk' + -ic; the chu- is not clear (Brasseur ch'u binic). xquicat 'they cut': x- + qui- 'they' + cat 'cut'. Ximénez writes plain c and Brasseur g (that is ꜫ); the verb is the certain q'at 'cut', and the toggle shows xkiq'at. vvapalil 'its main beam': v- + vapal + -il, taken as the ridge-beam with Brasseur ('master beam'); inferred.

sentences.t: Cate cut xbe ri Zipacna, xopon cu chila cuꜭ ri omuch ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: Then then went the Zipacna, arrived then there with-them the four-hundred boys.
sentences.i: Then Zipacna went and came up to the four hundred boys.
sentences.n: xbe 'he went', xopon 'he arrived (there)'. chila 'there'. cuꜭ 'with them': c- (qui- 'their' before a vowel) + uꜭ 'company', as ruꜭ 'with him'; the q-shaped letter is read ꜭ with Brasseur.

sentences.t: “Naquipa qui bano, ix ꜭaholab?” “Xa che maui ca ca yaco chi teleba.”
sentences.l: “What you-do, you boys?” “Only tree not we-lift to shoulder-carry.”
sentences.i: “What are you doing, boys?” “Only a tree that we cannot lift onto our shoulders.”
sentences.n: qui bano 'you (pl.) do': qui is c- (ongoing) + i- 'you (pl.)', the same letters as qui- 'their'. ix 'you (pl.)'. ca ca yaco 'we lift': ca (ongoing) + ca- 'we' + yac 'lift' + -o. chi teleba 'to carry it on the shoulder': teleb 'shoulder' (vteleb in the last part) with -a, which makes a verb of it.

sentences.t: “Xchin teleh. Apa copon vi? Naquipa vchac chi iꜭux?”
sentences.l: “I-shall shoulder-carry. Where it-reaches there? What its-work in your-heart?”
sentences.i: “I will carry it. Where is it to go? What do you have in mind for it?”
sentences.n: Xchin teleh 'I shall carry it on my shoulder': xchi- 'shall' + in 'I' + teleh, the verb of teleba. apa copon vi 'where does it get to': the manuscript runs apacopon together; it is divided as Brasseur divides it (a doubtful reading). copon 'it arrives (there)', the verb of xopon. vchac chi iꜭux 'its work in your heart': chac 'work', and iꜭux 'your (pl.) heart' (i- + ꜭux), the manuscript's chiiqux with a q-shaped letter read ꜭ; 'what do you want done with it?'.

sentences.t: “Xa vvapalil ca cabal.” “Vꜩ bala,” cha cut.
sentences.l: “Only its-ridge-beam our house.” “Good bala,” said then.
sentences.i: “Only the ridge-beam of our house.” “Very well,” he said.
sentences.n: ca cabal 'our house': ca- 'our'. cha 'he said': here the image has plain c, not the g of xꜭha, and it is printed as written (Brasseur cha).

sentences.t: Ta xuhuruh cut, xuteleba ca acanoc chu chi qui cabal omuch ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: Then he-hauled(?) then, he-shoulder-carried ca upward(?) at mouth their house four-hundred boys.
sentences.i: Then he heaved it up and carried it on his shoulder to the door of the four hundred boys' house.
sentences.n: xuhuruh 'he hauled it up': x- + v- 'he' + huruh, taken with hur 'drag' above (Brasseur 'he lifted it with force'); inferred. xuteleba 'he carried it on his shoulder'. ca acanoc is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has ca at the end of a line and acan oc on the next, and Brasseur prints cu akan-oc; acanoc is joined, as at the end of this part, and taken as 'upward', acan 'climb' (toggle aq'an, as in the earlier parts) + -oc. chu chi qui cabal 'at the mouth of their house', the doorway.

sentences.t: “Xa ta vi cat ꜭohe cuꜭ, at ꜭahol. Ꜭo pa a chuch, a cahau?” “Mahabi,” xꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “Only then there you-stay with-us, you boy. There-is (pa) your mother, your father?” “None,” he-said then.
sentences.i: “Then stay with us, boy. Have you a mother, a father?” “No,” he said.
sentences.n: cat ꜭohe 'you shall stay': c- + at 'you (one person)' + ꜭohe 'be, dwell'. cuꜭ 'with us': here c- is ca- 'our' before a vowel (q-), the same letters as cuꜭ 'with them' above; Brasseur prints kuq (his k is plain q), and the toggle shows quk'. at ꜭahol 'you, boy'. Ꜭo pa 'is there?': ꜭo 'there is', and pa is taken as a question word (Brasseur Qo-pa, 'have you?'); inferred. a chuch, a cahau 'your mother, your father': a- 'your (one person)'.

sentences.t: “Ca ca chaquimah tana bala chuvec chu vabaxic chic hun ca che racan ca cabal.” “Vꜩ,” xꜭha chi cut.
sentences.l: “We chaquimah(?) tana bala tomorrow to its-setting-up(?) again one our tree its-leg our house.” “Good,” he-said in-turn then.
sentences.i: “Tomorrow we will ask you again, to set up another tree, a post for our house.” “Good,” he said again.
sentences.n: chaquimah and tana are not otherwise known; Brasseur prints chakimah tanabala ('we shall take you again'), and 'we will ask you' is a guess. In chaquimah the letter is q-shaped where Brasseur has plain k (that is q), and it is printed qu; the toggle respells the letters. chuvec 'tomorrow'. chu vabaxic 'for its setting up': vabax, taken as 'set upright' + -ic, inferred. hun ca che racan ca cabal 'one of our trees, the leg of our house', another post. xꜭha chi cut 'he said in turn', chic with its c shared with cut.

sentences.t: Cate cut xcam qui naoh ri omuch ꜭaholab: “Are ri ala, hupacha chi ca ban chire chi ca camizah tah?
sentences.l: Then then took their thought the four-hundred boys: “This the youth, how that we-do to-him that we-kill (tah)?
sentences.i: Then the four hundred boys took counsel: “This young man here: what shall we do to him, so that we may kill him?
sentences.n: xcam qui naoh 'they took counsel', word for word 'took their thought': cam 'take' (Brasseur x-qam, read k'am), with qui- 'their' on naoh 'thought' and no prefix on the verb. ala 'youth, young man'. hupacha 'how'. chi ca ban chire 'that we do to him': the manuscript's chicaban could be read chicahan (b and h are alike here); b is printed, with Brasseur (chi ka ban), a doubtful reading. camizah 'kill': cam 'die' + -iz-, which makes 'cause to ...', + -ah, so 'make die'. tah after it marks the wish, 'so that we may'.

sentences.t: Rumal maui vꜩ ri cu bano; xa vtuquel mi xuyac ri che.
sentences.l: Because not good the he-does; only by-himself just-now he-lifted the tree.
sentences.i: For what he does is not good: he lifted the tree all by himself.
sentences.n: cu bano 'he does': c- (ongoing) + v- 'he' + bano. vtuquel 'by himself, alone'. mi 'just now'. xuyac 'he lifted': x- + v- 'he' + yac, the verb of yaco above. The four hundred fear his strength.

sentences.t: Ca coto hun nima hul; chiri ta cut chi ca ꜩac vi cahoc pa hul.
sentences.l: We-dig one great pit; there then then that we-drop there down in pit.
sentences.i: Let us dig a great pit; there we will drop him down into the pit.
sentences.n: Ca coto 'let us dig': ca- 'we' + cot 'dig' + -o. In every form of this verb in the part (coto, xucoto, vcotic, vcotobahic) Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur reads q (that is ꜭ); the toggle respells the letters as written. hul 'pit, hollow'. chi ca ꜩac 'that we let (him) fall': ꜩac 'fall', here with ca- 'we' and so transitive, 'drop'. cahoc 'downward': cah 'go down' + -oc.

sentences.t: Ha cama caha vleu pa hul, coh ꜭha ta chire.
sentences.l: ‘Go take(?) caha(?) earth in pit,’ we say then to-him.
sentences.i: ‘Go and take out the earth in the pit,’ we will say to him.
sentences.n: Here the boys rehearse the words they will say to Zipacna, quoted inside their own speech; the English sets them in single quotation marks, and coh ꜭha ta chire 'we will say to him' closes them. Ha is taken as 'go!', the command, after Brasseur ('Go and take...'), not ha 'water'. cama 'take' is inferred, as in the last part; caha is not otherwise known and may come from cah 'go down', but its sense here is a guess (Brasseur 'draw out'). coh ꜭha 'we say': c- + oh 'we' + ꜭha.

sentences.t: Chi are ta cut pachal cahoc pa hul, ta ca tarih cahoc ri nima che; chiri ta cut chi cam vi pa hul,” xeꜭha cut omuch ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: And this then then bent(?) down in pit, when we-let-go(?) down the great tree; there then then that he-die there in pit,” they-said then four-hundred boys.
sentences.i: And when he is bent over down in the pit, we will let the great tree fall down on him; and there he will die, in the pit,” said the four hundred boys.
sentences.n: pachal 'bent over' is taken as a word of position, after Brasseur ('once he is bent over and gone down into the pit'); inferred. Ximénez wrote an x before cahoc and blotted it out; it is not printed. ca tarih 'we let fall' is inferred from Brasseur ('we shall throw a great tree'); tarih is not otherwise known. chi cam vi 'that he die there': cam 'die' (modern kam), not cam 'take'.

sentences.t: Ta xquicot cut hun nima hul, naht xcahic.
sentences.l: Then they-dug then one great pit, far it-went-down.
sentences.i: Then they dug a great pit, and it went far down.
sentences.n: xquicot 'they dug': x- + qui- 'they' + cot 'dig', the verb of Ca coto. The same letters were xquicot 'they rejoiced' in the first part, a different verb; the toggle respells the letters in both. naht 'far' (nah in the earlier parts, here with a t). xcahic 'it went down': x- + cah + -ic.

sentences.t: Ta xquitac cut ri Zipacna: “Oh canih chavech; chi be ta a coto chic vleuh, maui ca ca rico,” xuchaxic.
sentences.l: Then they-sent then the Zipacna: “We canih(?) to-you; that go then you-dig more earth, not we-find(?),” he-was-told.
sentences.i: Then they sent for Zipacna: “We beg of you: go and dig out more of the earth; we cannot get to the bottom of it,” he was told.
sentences.n: xquitac 'they sent (for)': x- + qui- + tac 'send'. Oh canih chavech: Brasseur's note gives 'we love you', from canem 'love', and the king used the same words above ('I beg you'); here the sense is inferred, a word of entreaty. chavech 'to you (one person)': chi + av- 'your' (a- before a vowel) + ech. chi be ta a coto 'go and dig': a- 'you'. vleuh 'earth', with a final h, as in the earlier parts. maui ca ca rico 'we cannot find (it)', inferred: riq 'find'. xuchaxic 'he was told': x- + u- + cha 'say' + -x- (passive) + -ic, the u- standing in this passive as in xe vꜭhax 'they were told' in the second part; written here with plain ch; the toggle shows ch', as with chuchaxic in the last part.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala,” xꜭha cut. Cate cut xcah pa hul.
sentences.l: “Good bala,” he-said then. Then then went-down in pit.
sentences.i: “Very well,” he said. Then he went down into the pit.
sentences.n: xcah 'he went down', the verb of cahoc and xcahic.

sentences.t: “Ca ziquin vloc ta coto tahoc ri vleu; naht ta chi cahic avmal?” xuꜭhaxic.
sentences.l: “You-call hither when dug-out the earth; far then (chi) going-down by-you?” he-was-told.
sentences.i: “Call up to us when the earth has been dug out. Have you gone far down?” he was told.
sentences.n: ziquin 'call, shout' (modern sik'in, the verb of ziquih below): Ximénez writes qu, and the verb is certain, so the toggle restores the k'. ca is c- (ongoing) + a, perhaps a- 'you (one)' (Brasseur C'a ziquin), though with the intransitive ziquin one would expect cat 'you'; inferred. vloc 'hither', up to the boys. coto tahoc 'when (it) is dug': cot + -o + -tah + -oc, a passive (Brasseur qoto-tah-oc). avmal 'by you': av- 'your' + vmal, the umal of rumal 'by it'. Brasseur's French (damaged in the OCR here) gives of the first sentence only 'while he dug the earth'. xuꜭhaxic 'he was told', here with ꜭh.

sentences.t: “Ve,” xꜭha cut, ta xutiquiba vcotic hul; xa cu vhul xucoto vcolbal rib.
sentences.l: “Yes,” he-said then, when he-began its-digging pit; only then his-pit he-dug his-saving himself.
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, as he began to dig the pit; but the hole he dug was his own, to save himself.
sentences.n: Ve 'yes' (Brasseur 'yes'); the same letters as ve 'if' and ve 'my teeth'. xutiquiba 'he began': x- + v- 'he' + tiquiba 'plant, begin', the word of the preamble; the manuscript has xußquiba, the ß-ligature read ti. vcotic 'its digging' (MS vco-|ßc). xa cu vhul xucoto 'but his (own) hole he dug': vhul 'his hole' (v- + hul). vcolbal rib 'his means of saving himself': col 'save, free' + -bal, the ending of means, with rib 'himself'.

sentences.t: Xretamah ri vcamizaxic; ta xucot cut hun vi chi hul chu ꜩalanem; vca hul xuticoto, xcolotah vi.
sentences.l: He-knew the his-being-killed; then he-dug then one again(?) pit at side(?); its-second pit he-began-digging(?), was-saved there.
sentences.i: He knew that they meant to kill him; so he dug another pit at the side; a second pit he dug, and in it he was safe.
sentences.n: xretamah 'he knew': x- + r- 'he' (before a vowel) + etamah 'know'. vcamizaxic 'his being killed': camiz 'kill' + -ax- (passive) + -ic. hun vi chi hul: the manuscript has hun|vichihul, divided as Brasseur divides it; 'another pit' is inferred. chu ꜩalanem 'at the side' follows Brasseur ('to the side'); ꜩalanem is not otherwise known. vca hul 'a second pit': vca, taken as vcab 'its second' without its b. xuticoto: the manuscript has xußcoto, and Brasseur x-u qoto; it may be xutic coto 'he began to dig', and it is printed as written (a doubtful reading). xcolotah 'he was saved': col 'save' + -otah, inferred, as in xcolo 'was freed' in the first part (Brasseur x-colo-tah).

sentences.t: “Ca hanican pala?” xuꜭhax cu cahoc cumal omuch ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: “(Ca) how-far(?) pala(?)?” he-was-told then downward by-them four-hundred boys.
sentences.i: “How far along are you?” the four hundred boys called down to him.
sentences.n: hanican pala is taken as a question 'how much, how far' (Brasseur 'is it nearly done?'); hanican is not otherwise known, and pala is the second half of a question word in the third part (haruh pala). Both are inferred. xuꜭhax cu cahoc 'he was told then, down (into the pit)': xuꜭhax, the passive, without its -ic before the words that follow.

sentences.t: “Qui na nu coto; ve xquix nu ziquih acanoc, ta chuꜩinoc vcotobahic,” xcha vloc Zipacna chiri pa hul.
sentences.l: “I still my-digging; if you(pl.)-shall I-call upward, when let-it-be-finished its-digging,” said hither Zipacna there in pit.
sentences.i: “I am still digging; I will call up to you when the digging is finished,” Zipacna called up from there in the pit.
sentences.n: The manuscript runs quinanucoto ve xquix nuzi-|quih together; it is divided and punctuated as Brasseur prints it. Qui na nu coto 'I (am) still digging': qui taken as c- + i(n) 'I', its n not written (as quiꜭohe 'I am' in the earlier parts), na 'still', nu coto 'my digging'; inferred. xquix nu ziquih 'I shall call you (pl.)': xquix is xc- 'shall' + ix 'you (pl.)', the object, and nu- 'I', the subject of ziquih 'call' (modern sik'ij). acanoc 'upward', as above. chuꜩinoc 'let it be finished': ch- + vꜩin 'be finished' + -oc. vcotobahic 'its digging out': cot 'dig' + -obah + -ic. xcha 'he said': again plain ch in the image (Brasseur cha). vloc 'hither', up from the pit. The part ends here, with Zipacna's answer from below; his escape continues in the next part.
